title: Warsh Fed Cements Higher-for-Longer Before Soft June Payrolls Cloud the Hike Path
content: The hawkish regime under new chair Kevin Warsh remained the window's dominant cross-asset force. June's FOMC held at 3.50-3.75% but a terser statement, stripped forward guidance and an upgraded SEP, with 2026 PCE lifted toward 3.6% and growth trimmed, pushed several officials to pencil in hikes. Markets took the cue: the 2-year UST yield jumped around 16bp on the day, its largest Fed-day move since 2008, and implied odds of a December hike climbed toward 80%, while the USD firmed to a one-year high. Late in the window a soft June payrolls print near 57k, well below consensus, with unemployment around 4.2%, reintroduced two-sided risk, trimming hike bets and lifting gold toward $4,200. The tension between sticky inflation and cooling labour left rates, FX and rate-sensitive equities hostage to each release.

title: Great Rotation Deepens as Semiconductors Sell Off and the Dow Sets Records
content: Equity leadership kept broadening away from the mega-cap AI complex that led the first half. As the window closed the PHLX Semiconductor Index shed more than 12% in a handful of sessions, unwinding part of an 80%-plus first-half surge as investors banked profits on stretched positioning and questioned the payback on AI capex. Capital rotated into the real economy, favouring industrials, financials, energy and consumer staples, driving the Dow to record highs even as the Nasdaq and S&P 500 consolidated or slipped. Market breadth improved as leadership widened beyond a handful of names. Higher-for-longer rates compounded the shift by pressuring long-duration growth multiples, while cyclicals drew support from a resilient activity backdrop. The rotation persisted across all four weeks and was read as a healthier, less concentrated regime rather than a broad risk-off.

title: Middle East De-escalation and OPEC+ Supply Drag Oil Back to Pre-War Levels
content: The energy risk premium that had gripped markets through the Hormuz crisis unwound decisively over the window, easing a key inflation swing factor. A US-Iran framework and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz let Gulf supply rebuild, with Saudi and UAE exports recovering toward pre-war baselines and flows through the strait climbing back above 10m b/d. OPEC+ approved a fourth consecutive quota increase, roughly 600k b/d cumulatively, against a downgraded 2026 demand outlook. Brent drifted from its conflict highs toward the low-$70s, near levels last seen before the February escalation, with WTI dipping below $70. The slide was not linear, as a cargo-ship attack near Oman and the abrupt postponement of Geneva talks produced brief spikes, but the dominant direction was lower. Falling crude eased headline-inflation fears and helped cap long-end yields while weighing on energy equities.
